name: Omar Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the laying side of a free-range egg farm, 16,000 hens in two sheds. I'm in by half six to walk the sheds before the lights come fully up, because that's when you spot a hen that's off colour. Then it's checking the belt that carries the eggs to the packing room, the water lines, the feed bins, and getting the birds out onto the range once it's light.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is a quiet shed in the morning, all the birds talking to each other in that low murmur. Worst is bird flu season. Twice now we've had to keep them all inside for months, and you spend every day waiting for a phone call that says a farm down the road has it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Leila, who teaches at the primary school in the village. We're saving for a wedding, slowly. Very slowly. We've got about two weeks of money put by, because my wage is low for what I do and the egg packer's contract hasn't gone up in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool, use it when it helps. I already ask one of those chat programs to tidy up my emails to the packer sometimes, because I write like a farmer. Nothing much to post about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it changes very little. The packer still pays us a price per dozen that doesn't cover the feed rise, and AI won't change that. I'd keep using it for the odd letter and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep asking the owner, Mrs Achterberg, to push the packer for a better price at the contract review in March. And I'd keep putting the forty a month into the wedding pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing on this card keeps me up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you write like a farmer. What does the program actually do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It turns 'eggs cracked too much, belt problem, fixed Tuesday' into three polite sentences. Leila used to do that for me. Now she gets her evenings back, which she's very happy about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who's scared of these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say try it on something boring and low stakes first, like a letter. That's what I did. If it's rubbish, you've lost five minutes.

S0.say: I'd say it's a tool, so use it when it helps. I already use one to tidy up my emails to the egg packer, and there's nothing much to post about.
S0.think: It changes very little for me. The packer's price per dozen still doesn't cover rising feed costs, and AI won't fix that.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for the odd letter. Asks the owner to push the packer for a better price at the March contract review, and keeps saving forty a month for the wedding.
S0.quote: It turns 'eggs cracked too much, belt problem, fixed Tuesday' into three polite sentences.
S0.fieldNote: Omar is practical and measured, a careful adopter who tried AI on low-stakes letters first. His frustration is with the egg packer's contract price, not technology. He's easy and funny when talking about his partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a slow change, so there's time to get the training right. I'd probably say that the government should make sure young people still get a first job, because that's how you learn. You can't learn chickens from a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly fine. The bit that worries me is the vets and the packing room. If the packer stops hiring junior graders and uses cameras instead, fine, but the two women who grade our eggs are in their fifties and this is the only work near here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd read up on the camera grading systems, once a couple of other farms had them, so I'm not caught out. I'd talk to Grace and Tomasz, our part-timers, about what other work they could pick up on the farm. Probably the range and the hedges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. It's the people around me more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are Grace and Tomasz?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace does the packing room four mornings a week, and Tomasz does the heavy lifting, muck-outs between flocks, that sort of thing. Grace has worked here longer than I have. I'm technically her boss, which still feels strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you take up a new system yourself, early or late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the middle. I'd let a bigger farm make the mistakes first, then go and look at theirs. That's how we did the new feed system. I went and stood in a shed in the next county for an afternoon before we spent a penny.

S1.say: I'd say it's slow enough that there's time to do training properly. The government should make sure young people still get a first job, because you can't learn chickens from a video.
S1.think: I'm mostly fine myself. My worry is the packing room staff, who are in their fifties and have no other work nearby if cameras take over the grading.
S1.do: Reads up on camera grading once a couple of other farms have it. Talks to his two part-timers about other farm work they could take on, such as the range and the hedges.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, mainly for his part-time staff.
S1.quote: I went and stood in a shed in the next county for an afternoon before we spent a penny.
S1.fieldNote: His 'wait and look' approach is very clear and clearly works for him. He feels responsible for Grace even though she's older than him. His politics show in the call for guaranteed first jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the politicians should stop shouting and protect the people losing jobs: proper redundancy pay, proper retraining. I'd share that sort of thing online, not my own long rants, just articles. I'm not much of a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worry is Leila. Schools have office staff too, and if the office goes, she'll be doing parent letters till nine at night. And people being laid off means cheaper eggs win in the shops, and free range is the first thing families drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Mrs Achterberg and look at what happens if egg sales drop by ten percent. I'd also ask the packer what they're seeing, because they always know first. And I'd move the wedding back a year, I think, if money looked tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the weather's turning but it hasn't rained yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving the wedding back. Would that be a hard conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. Leila's mum has already been looking at halls. I'd probably start by showing her the numbers, because she's better with numbers than me, and let her come to it herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at any of the new AI-related jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. They're in cities, and I'm good at this. Maybe if there was something like farm data work I could do from here, but I'd want to see someone else do it first.

S2.say: I'd say politicians should stop shouting and protect laid-off people with proper redundancy pay and retraining. I'd share articles online rather than write my own posts.
S2.think: My real worry is Leila doing the school office work at night, and families switching to cheaper eggs when money is tight. Free range is the first thing people drop.
S2.do: Works out with the owner what a ten percent fall in egg sales would mean. Asks the packer what trends they see, and considers pushing the wedding back a year.
S2.feel: Uneasy, like bad weather is coming but hasn't arrived.
S2.quote: Like the weather's turning but it hasn't rained yet.
S2.fieldNote: The threat reaches him indirectly, through his partner's school and through shoppers trading down. Postponing the wedding was the concrete cost that made it real. He again wants proof before considering any new kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need strong unions and a proper tax on these companies. People who own shares and houses get richer while everyone else loses their job. I'd go to a march, maybe, if there was one in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the hens still need someone, so I'm alright for now. But Leila and I rent, and if house prices boom, rents follow. We'd never buy. That's the bit that makes me angry: I do a real job, and the only way to get on is to already own something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the wedding and start saving for rent instead, honestly. I'd ask Mrs Achterberg if there's any chance of the empty farm cottage, even if it needs work. And I'd join the union properly instead of just meaning to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and quite angry. The work's fine, but the life around it gets harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to a march maybe. What would make it a yes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Leila came, honestly. And if it was a weekend, because the hens don't take days off. I went to one about farm pay years ago and had to leave at two to be back for lock-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would people with money from shares buy more expensive eggs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, yes. The farm shop in the market town might sell more of our eggs to people with new money. But it's a small slice. Most of what we do goes to the packer and into supermarket boxes.

S3.say: I'd say this is why we need strong unions and a proper tax on these companies. Shareholders and homeowners get richer while others lose their jobs.
S3.think: The hens still need me, so the job is safe for now. But rents will follow house prices, and it makes me angry that only people who already own something can get on.
S3.do: Switches his savings from the wedding to rent. Asks the owner about the empty farm cottage even if it needs work, and finally joins the union.
S3.feel: Anxious and angry; the work is fine but life around it gets harder.
S3.quote: I went to one about farm pay years ago and had to leave at two to be back for lock-up.
S3.fieldNote: The anger is about housing and fairness, not his own job. He stays practical even here: the wedding fund becomes the rent fund. The march story neatly shows how the hens fence in his whole life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules: robots in farms only if the workers share in what's saved, and only if animal welfare checks still have a trained person signing them. I'd say it at the union and probably online this time. This one's about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think a lot of my job could go. The belts are already automatic. If a robot can walk the shed, pick up floor eggs and pull out dead birds, that's half of Tomasz's job and a third of mine. I'd still be needed to manage it, maybe, but they wouldn't need both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see the robots working on another farm before anything else, like always. Then I'd go to Mrs Achterberg and offer to be the one who runs them, and ask for training paid by her or by the company selling them. And I'd be honest with Tomasz early, so he has time to look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first card where I picture myself in the job centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be honest with Tomasz early. What would you actually say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like, 'I don't know yet, but I won't let you hear it from someone else.' He's got a little girl. He deserves months, not a week's notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two weeks of savings, how long could you and Leila manage if your pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On her wage alone, we'd pay the rent and eat, and that's it. The car would go, and I'd have to find something within cycling distance, which round here is nothing. So maybe a few months before it really bit.

S4.say: I'd say robots on farms need rules: workers should share in the savings, and a trained person should still sign off animal welfare checks. This time I'd say it online as well, because it's about me.
S4.think: A lot of my job could go. If robots can walk the shed, pick up floor eggs and remove dead birds, the owner wouldn't need both me and Tomasz.
S4.do: Visits another farm to see the robots working first, then offers to run them himself if the owner or supplier pays for training. Tells his part-time worker early so he has time to look for other work.
S4.feel: Alarmed; it's the first time he pictures himself at the job centre.
S4.quote: He's got a little girl. He deserves months, not a week's notice.
S4.fieldNote: Robots hit him directly, and his tone changes from measured to worried. Even so, he stays steady: see it working, then offer to run it. His first thought is still for the worker under him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, easily. What would help is training paid for by whoever profits from the machines, and a rule that a trained person checks the animals. And honestly, cheaper rent. If housing wasn't eating us alive, a job change wouldn't be so scary.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about bird flu. Every farmer I know thinks more about disease than about AI. If a robot could keep the flu out, I'd have one tomorrow.

headlineQuote: It's the first card where I picture myself in the job centre.
portrait: Omar Tanaka is 27 and runs a 16,000-hen free-range egg unit, living in a rented home with his partner Leila, a primary school teacher, and saving slowly for their wedding. He's careful and good-humoured, and he only takes up new things after he has seen them work on someone else's farm. The early scenarios barely touch him; what bothers him is the packer's price, rising rent and his partner's workload. Robots in the last scenario hit him directly, and he pictures losing his job for the first time. Even then he plans to see it working, offer to run it, and warn his part-time worker early.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because robots could take over much of his job and his part-time worker's job in the hen sheds.
whatWouldHelp: Training paid for by whoever profits from the machines, a rule that trained people check the animals, and cheaper rent.
